Lessons.Title: Whole Numbers and Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Source 2021 warm-up Notice and Wonder: Four Number Lines. The ORIGINAL first diagram shows four co-located scales spanning the same 0–3 wholes: whole steps 0 to 3, halves 0 to 6/2, thirds 0 to 9/3, fourths 0 to 12/4. These are different names for the same positions of 1, 2, 3; accept multiple student observations and questions with teacher review, not a fixed odd-one-out.

Activity1 Hidden Whole Numbers: on original 0–6/2, 0–9/3 and 0–12/4 lines, circle fraction positions exactly at WHOLE-number ticks; the first whole is 2/2=3/3=4/4=1, the second 4/2=6/3=8/4=2 and the third 6/2=9/3=12/4=3. Original teacher shows 4/2=2 and students must write FIVE OTHER distinct equations for fractions at whole numbers; many valid sets, so preserve student selection and teacher checks.

Activity1 six separate SOURCE yes/no fraction checks: 11/2=5.5 NOT a whole number; 5/1=5 YES; 12/6=2 YES; 10/3=3+1/3 NOT whole; 12/8=1+1/2 NOT whole; 16/4=4 YES. Fractions are whole exactly when the denominator divides numerator without remainder. Be careful not to classify 'numerator > denominator' as sufficient for a whole or treat 12/8 as a whole.

Activity2 Write Them as Fractions is a cooperative THREE-COLUMN TABLE with top whole numbers exactly 4, 5, 6. In Step1, each pupil writes two fractions equivalent to EACH whole number: SIX entries across those columns, then passes the paper right. Step2 participants add one NEW valid fraction to a chosen column and pass again, repeating to complete the table. There is NO single fixed full table: the original student sheet preprints 4/1 under 4, 30/6 under 5 and 48/8 under 6 as anchors, and offers denominator rows including 2, 3 and 4. Accept all n/d matching 4, 5 or 6, with d>0, consistent with original group workflow.

First-party table examples 4=4/1=8/2=12/3=16/4; 5=5/1=10/2=15/3=20/4=30/6; 6=6/1=12/2=18/3=24/4=48/8 are illustrative, not imposed as student answers. Teachers check that the paper was rotated, students wrote new valid entries, and any repeated forms fit the actual whole-number column.

Source section summary also illustrates 3/4=6/8 on a 0–1 line and that whole numbers can be represented as fractions. Public teacher and preparation HTML, along with eleven unique image URLs, were inspected on Our-CS; source publisher artwork or photography are not copied. The original publisher Cool-down Fraction to Whole Number and Whole Number to Fraction is gated and was not retrieved; neither original student task PDF nor runtime or tests were certified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole numbers as fractional points
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every whole number k is a fraction kn/n for any positive integer n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number criterion
KeyConcepts.Definition: A nonzero denominator yields a whole number exactly if it divides the numerator.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a/b is whole if a mod b =0 for positive integers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed whole across multiple number lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: One unit always occupies the same length across differently partitioned aligned number lines.

KeyConcepts.Title: Open group-generated fraction table
KeyConcepts.Definition: A whole-number column can contain many equivalent fractions, not one exact answer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For whole k and chosen positive denominator d, numerator is kd.

WorkedExamples.Title: Aligned fraction number lines
WorkedExamples.Question: Locate one, two and three on halves, thirds and fourths lines.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts per whole, twice for two and three times for three.
WorkedExamples.Check: All source lines span zero to three.

WorkedExamples.Title: Six exact whole-number checks
WorkedExamples.Question: Which of 11/2,5/1,12/6,10/3,12/8,16/4 are whole?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide numerator by denominator and examine remainder.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original group table
WorkedExamples.Question: Generate several fractions in columns for 4,5 and6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply chosen positive denominator by each column's whole number.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Multiple valid tables; no fixed complete response
WorkedExamples.Check: Preserve printed anchors 4/1,30/6,48/8 and student contribution.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 11/2 or 12/8 as whole numbers because numerator exceeds denominator.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check divisibility; remainder must be zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Divide a 0–3 entire line into six equal pieces and call the first 1/2 of the unit.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Six intervals over three whole units have size 1/2, but the first unit itself must have TWO intervals and ends at tick 2.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the 0–1 unit consistent across all aligned scales.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Require one predetermined fraction for the group table or FIVE exact equations.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks pupils to generate valid choices, explain and pass their paper.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Grade validity and distinctness where requested; teacher verifies participation.

SummaryPoints: Activity1 4/2=2 plus five OTHER examples; any legitimate whole-number fractions acceptable.
Six source checks: NO 11/2, YES 5/1, YES 12/6, NO 10/3, NO 12/8, YES 16/4.
Activity2 group table anchors 4/1,30/6,48/8 in columns 4,5,6; many valid entries with passing right.
Visuals need teacher comparison. Publisher student PDF, Cool-down, tests and Stage D deferred.
